papers.title: Min-CSPs on Complete Instances III: Nearly Optimal Characterizations of Approximation for Symmetric CSPs
papers.abstract: This paper studies complete Min-$k$-CSPs: an instance on $n$ variables has one nontrivial constraint for every $k$-set of variables (so $\binom{n}{k}$ constraints in total), and the goal is to find an assignment that minimizes the number of unsatisfied constraints. They are motivated by the connections to machine learning and data science, as well as the possibility of being testbeds for new algorithmic techniques. Previous recent results presented polynomial-time algorithms for the decision version of every complete Boolean $k$-CSP, which is a necessary condition for any multiplicative approximations for the minimization version, but nontrivial approximation results have been limited to fragile CSPs, 2-SAT, and NAE-3-SAT, leaving the approximability of most complete Boolean Min-CSPs open, including complete Min-$k$-SAT. In this paper, we resolve this question, up to nearly matching factors, for the natural class of symmetric Boolean predicates. Given $A \subseteq \{0, \dots, k\}$, Min-CSP($A$) is a Min-$k$-CSP where each constraint is specified by $k$ literals and is satisfied if the number of true literals belongs to $A$. Let $w(A)$ be the maximum number of consecutive integers in $A$. Our main results for complete Min-CSP($A$) are (1) a QPTAS for $w(A) \leq 2$ and (2) an $\widetilde{O}(n^{w(A)-3})$-approximation for $w(A) \geq 3$, as well as almost matching hardness results for the latter. Our QPTAS for $w(A)=2$ significantly improves the previous $O(1)$-approximation for Min-2-SAT and the $\operatorname{polylog}(n)$-approximation for Min-NAE-3-SAT, as well as extends the PTAS for fragile CSPs (i.e., $w(A) = 1$).

papers.title: What to Predict for Efficient Scheduling on Parallel Machines
papers.abstract: We study learning-augmented algorithms for scheduling on multiple parallel machines under the objectives of minimizing the makespan or the total weighted completion time. We assume that the algorithm has access to noisy information (the prediction) about an optimal solution, expressed through a solution encoding that implicitly quantifies both the amount of information provided and the nature of noise (errors in the prediction). Our central question is to determine the maximum level of noise that still allows for efficiently recovering this optimal solution. We observe that information guiding greedy scheduling to optimality or revealing the optimal assignment of tasks to machines is very sensitive to noise, and prove that recovering an optimal solution from solution encodings capturing either is computationally hard, even for a small (non-constant) number of errors. On the positive side, we show that an order-based encoding, which leads to errors that are dispersed locally, is robust to noise. We present a dynamic programming framework that utilizes this encoding and solves optimally several classical scheduling problems, including makespan and total weighted completion time minimization on identical or unrelated machines.

papers.title: Artificial Currency and Separate Selling: A 3-Approximation for Consumer Surplus
papers.abstract: We study the allocation of indivisible items to buyers with additive values drawn from independent distributions. The objective is consumer surplus net of burnt payments. We consider artificial-currency mechanisms: buyers receive personalized budgets of a currency worthless outside the mechanism and use them to bid across items. The better of separate selling and artificial-currency mechanisms provides a 3-approximation to optimal consumer surplus. The guarantee holds at every Bayes--Nash equilibrium, without equilibrium selection. Both branches are necessary: either alone may capture only a vanishing share of the optimum. The proof decomposes benchmark surplus into a stable part captured by artificial currency and a variation covered by separate selling.

papers.title: Online Graph Coloring: Competitive Ratios Separating Randomized and Deterministic Algorithms
papers.abstract: We study online coloring, focusing on the competitive ratio. The best previously known results were (1) a lower bound of $Ω(n / \log^2 n)$ for both deterministic and randomized algorithms by Halldórsson and Szegedy (1994), (2) an upper bound of $O(n / \log n)$ for randomized algorithms by Halldórsson (1997), and (3) an upper bound of $O(n / \log \log n)$ for deterministic algorithms by Kawarabayashi, Yoneda, and Yoneda (2025). In this paper, we improve these results as follows: 1. A new lower bound of $Ω(n / \log n)$ for deterministic algorithms. 2. A new upper bound of $O(n (\log \log n)^2 / \log^2 n)$ for randomized algorithms. 3. A new upper bound of $O(n / (\log \log n)^{2-\varepsilon})$ for deterministic algorithms for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$. For randomized algorithms, we nearly close the gap between the lower and upper bounds; the remaining gap is only $O((\log \log n)^2)$. We establish the asymptotic separation between randomized and deterministic online graph coloring. Against an oblivious adversary, a polynomial-time randomized algorithm achieves a competitive ratio asymptotically smaller than any deterministic algorithm can guarantee, even with unlimited computation.

papers.title: Real-Time String Indexing in Optimal Time
papers.abstract: In this paper we describe the first fully real-time indexing solution for pattern matching over an arbitrary integer alphabet. Our data structure spends $O(1)$ worst-case time w.h.p. for processing each new letter appended to $T$ and worst-case $O(|P|+occ)$ time for reporting all occurrences of $P$, where $T$ and $P$ are strings over an integer alphabet. The main idea of our solution is a novel representation of the suffix tree, the path-decomposed suffix tree, which does not store the full topology of the suffix tree but instead decomposes it into paths, each stored in a dictionary that encodes parent--child relationships indirectly.

papers.title: Approximating graphic TSP by b-matchings
papers.abstract: We give a polynomial-time algorithm for graphic TSP that returns a tour of length at most $\frac{89}{64}=\frac{7}{5}-\frac{3}{320}$ times the value of the subtour relaxation. This improves the long-standing ratio $\frac75$ of Sebő and Vygen and shows that the integrality gap of the subtour LP on graphic instances is at most $\frac{89}{64}\approx 1.3906$. We optimize a non-linear objective function over an odd-join polytope, which uses (i) a new removable system of edges, and (ii) reconnection of subtours if the graph is disconnected. This approach gives a $\frac{13}{10}$-approximation algorithm for $4$-regular $4$-vertex-connected graphs, improving the $\frac43$ of Newman, and a $\frac43$-approximation for $k$-vertex-connected graphs of maximum degree at most $k+1$, for every $k\ge 3$. For the general graphic TSP, we construct a feasible point in the odd-join polytope, using an optimal vertex from the Subtour linear programming relaxation of TSP, which helps us bound the approximation factor by 89/64.

papers.title: Feedback Vertex Set, Max Cut, and Edge Coloring on the Strong Product of a Graph and a Path
papers.abstract: We examine the computational complexity of well-known problems on subgraphs of the strong product of two paths. Namely, for Max Cut we show NP-hardness on induced subgraphs of $P \boxtimes P$ answering a question by Dvořák, Huynh, Joret, Liu, and Wood (2021). For 3-Edge Coloring we show NP-hardness on subgraphs of $P \boxtimes P$ and that it is equivalent to 3-Edge Coloring on planar graphs for induced subgraphs of $P \boxtimes P$. It is a long standing open question whether 3-Edge Coloring on planar graphs is NP-hard. As a second contribution, we consider graphs of the form $G \boxtimes P$ and show that Feedback Vertex Set on these graphs is FPT in the clique-width of $G$. Furthermore, we show that it can be solved in polynomial time if $G$ is chordal or co-comparable and that the computational complexity depends on the parity of $P$ if $G$ is bipartite. Namely, it is solvable in polynomial time if $P$ has an even number of vertices but is NP-complete otherwise. For Max Cut, we show that it can be solved in polynomial time if $G$ is bipartite.

papers.title: Second-Best Trade Is Half Efficient in Multidimensional Markets
papers.abstract: We prove that at least half of the first-best gains from trade can always be achieved in multidimensional two-sided markets with additive values and costs and arbitrary downward-closed feasibility constraints. The guarantee is achieved by a mechanism satisfying Bayesian incentive compatibility, interim individual rationality, and strong budget balance, and is tight already in single-item bilateral trade. Types are independent across agents, while the coordinates of each agent's type may be arbitrarily correlated. Feasibility constraints may couple trades across items and agents. This extends the known tight one-half guarantee for single-item bilateral trade. Our proof develops a new application of the Cai--Devanur--Weinberg duality framework. We show that the objective of every feasible dual is at least half of the first best. Strong duality then yields the guarantee without characterizing an optimal mechanism or dual. The key observation is that every feasible dual induces continuous-time Markov chains that, when stopped by exponential clocks, recover true types as expectations of virtual types. The dual constraints control the rate at which these chains change the prior distributions. We establish our bound by combining this control with a coupling of the agents' clocks.

papers.title: Characterizing Fixed-Treewidth Planar Graphs
papers.abstract: We give the first inductive characterization of planar graphs of treewidth $k$ for each $k \geq 3$. Our definition generalizes the well-known inductive definition of planar $3$-trees and the recent definition of so-called planar quasi-$4$-trees [Förster, 2024]. As a key step, which may be of independent interest, we show that every planar triangulation $G$ of treewidth $k$ admits a tree decomposition of width $k$ where each adhesion set induces a cycle in $G$. As an application of planar quasi-$4$-trees, we show that planar graphs of treewidth at most $4$ have vertex arboricity at most $2$. That is, the vertex-set of every planar graph of treewidth at most $4$ can be partitioned into two sets that each induce a forest.

papers.title: Bounding and Approximating Kostka Numbers
papers.abstract: Kostka numbers, the coefficients of Schur polynomials, count semistandard Young tableaux of prescribed shape and weight. We give a deterministic algorithm for approximating Kostka numbers within a simply exponential factor in the number of variables and the size of the partition. Our approach combines Gurvits capacity bounds for log-concave polynomials with an algorithm for approximating the Gurvits capacity of a Schur polynomial. For a Schur polynomial in $n$ variables indexed by $λ$, we show that the logarithm of the capacity associated with any nonzero coefficient can be approximated to additive error $ε$ in time polynomial in $n$, $|λ|$, and $\log(1/ε)$. The analysis establishes an explicit bounded optimization region and efficient approximate first-order oracles, and handles boundary weights through a factorization into smaller Schur polynomials.

papers.title: Improved Bounds for Online Matching with Random Edge Arrivals
papers.abstract: We study the unweighted online matching problem with random edge arrivals, where each edge arrives at an independent time drawn uniformly from $[0,1]$, and the algorithm must immediately and irrevocably accept or reject it while maintaining a matching. Guruganesh and Singla (IPCO, 2017) first broke the $1/2$ barrier of the naive Greedy algorithm by giving a $(1/2+\varepsilon)$-competitive algorithm for a small constant $\varepsilon>0$, a guarantee that has remained the best known for nearly a decade. We give a simple three-phase algorithm that achieves a competitive ratio of $0.5445$ by deliberately rejecting selected early edges to reserve their endpoints for later matching opportunities. With a different choice of parameters, the same algorithm is $0.5535$-competitive on triangle-free graphs, including bipartite graphs. We also establish competitive ratio upper bounds below $0.6964$ for general graphs and $0.7043$ for bipartite graphs via exact rational evaluation of an optimal-policy recurrence on fixed graphs, even when the input graph is known up to isomorphism.

papers.title: Nonadaptive One-Sided Testing of Binary Rank
papers.abstract: The binary rank of a binary matrix is the minimum number of disjoint all-one rectangles that partition its one-entries. We study entry-query testing of binary rank at most $d$, with one-sided error and nonadaptive queries. We give a tester using $\tilde O(d^4/ε^2)$ queries, independent of the matrix dimensions and a general lower bound of $\tilde Ω(d^{3/2}/ε)$.

papers.title: Rotating Walks, Derandomized Squares, and Permutation Conjugated Walks
papers.abstract: Using the recent strong convergence results of Bordenave and Collins (Annals of Mathematics) and Chen et al. (Annals of Mathematics), we study the average case behavior of rotating random walks of Cohen and Maor (STOC 2023) and the derandomized square construction of Rozenman and Vadhan (RANDOM 2005). Concretely, we prove a conjecture of Cohen et al. (ITCS 2025) regarding the average case behavior of derandomized squaring for random graphs and show that the existential bounds of Cohen and Maor for their rotating random walk construction hold with high-probability for random graphs. Using the results of O'Donnell and Wu (FOCS 2020), we can in polynomial time construct a family of graphs and rotations which almost saturate the bounds of Cohen and Maor, and meet the bounds conjectured by Cohen et al. for all vertex-transitive auxiliary graphs of fixed degree in the derandomized square. Finally, we study independent random permutation conjugates of deterministic regular graph adjacency matrices. We prove quantitative weak convergence to freely independent tree adjacency operators when the degrees are fixed and the girths tend to infinity. Separately, a covering argument gives deterministic spectral lower bounds for polynomials with non-negative coefficients, recovering the lower bound of Cohen et al. for rotating walks.

papers.title: Minimum Membership Dominating Set and Its Generalization: Leafage vs. Asteroidal Number
papers.abstract: The Dominating Set problem is known to be fixed-parameter tractable when parameterized by leafage, a structural graph parameter defined on chordal graphs. We investigate whether this tractability extends to its variants with natural constraints. Specifically, we study the Minimum Membership Dominating Set problem and its generalization, the Min. $(σ, ρ)$-Dominating Set problem. Given a graph $G$ and a positive integer $\ell$, Minimum Membership Dominating Set asks whether there is a dominating set $D$ such that every vertex in $G$ is dominated by at most $\ell$ vertices in $D$. We first show a negative result: Minimum Membership Dominating Set parameterized by leafage plus $\ell$ is W[1]-hard, demonstrating that even this natural constraint serves as a severe barrier to designing FPT algorithms. To complement this, we present an XP algorithm for the Min. $(σ, ρ)$-Dominating Set problem parameterized by asteroidal number plus $μ$, where $σ$ and $ρ$ are finite sets of non-negative integers and $μ$ is the maximum value in $σ\cup ρ$. Note that asteroidal number generalizes leafage to arbitrary graphs. Combining this algorithm with our structural bound that every graph $G$ admits a dominating set such that no vertex is dominated by more than $7\mathsf{an}(G)-6$ vertices, where $\mathsf{an}(G)$ denotes the asteroidal number of $G$, we show that Minimum Membership Dominating Set admits an XP algorithm parameterized solely by asteroidal number.

papers.title: Greedy+Singleton for knapsack-constrained monotone submodular maximization has approximation ratio exactly $β^\star \approx 0.42944$
papers.abstract: Greedy+Singleton is the textbook heuristic for monotone submodular maximization under a knapsack constraint: it returns the better of the cost-benefit greedy set and the best single item. Its worst-case approximation ratio, known only to lie in $[0.427, 0.42945]$ (Feldman-Nutov-Shoham; Kulik-Schwartz-Shachnai), is exactly an explicit constant $β^\star\approx 0.42944$. In the extremal instances, many cheap "filler" items wear down the value of two large optimal items while greedy spends the budget, until neither fits. This picture gives a sharper factor-revealing relaxation; we bound it analytically near the extremal parameters, up to finitely many interval-arithmetic checks, and certify it elsewhere by an exact branch-and-bound. The matching bad instances are tie-free and checkable by hand. For the version that stops at the first item that does not fit, Wolsey's bound $1-e^{-β_W}\approx 0.35780$, where $e^{β_W}=2-β_W$, is tight; Wolsey stated this for his variant without giving the instances, and we give an explicit family with no ties that also covers comparison with the best feasible singleton. The CELF rule also has ratio exactly $β^\star$.

papers.title: Parameterized Complexity and Geometric Approximation of Riesz Energy Subset Selection
papers.abstract: We choose $k$ of $n$ sites to minimize Riesz $s$-energy, in which a pair at distance $t$ contributes $t^{-s}$. For $s=2$, exact selection is polynomial on a line but NP-hard in the plane. Adapting the proxy lemma of Ceccarello et al. gives an efficient parameterized approximation scheme (EPAS) for fixed Euclidean dimension and fixed $s>0$. To sharpen the bound, we start with a geometric packing. Farthest-first traversal gives $2k$ centers separated by at least the last insertion distance $r$. If one site of an optimum is removed, each of the $k-1$ remaining sites excludes at most one center closer than $r/2$, leaving at least $k+1$ centers free. The new step is a discrete exchange bound: the removed site's interaction energy is at most the average it would contribute at those free centers. In the plane at $s=2$, this reduces the representative bound from $O(k^2\log(2k)/\varepsilon^2)$ for a packing estimate of total energy to $O(k\log(2k)/\varepsilon^2)$, independently of $n$. Rational planar examples show that the resulting separation scale $r/\sqrt{\log(2k)}$ is sharp. A $(1+\varepsilon)$ approximation on rational planar sites takes $O(nk+n\log n)+(C\log(2k)/\varepsilon^2)^k$ operations of polynomial bit cost. The observed number $M$ of representatives determines the search size $\binom{M}{k}$. With one million sites, $k=5$ and $\varepsilon=1/2$, the exchange grid left 252 subsets on clustered inputs and about $9.3\times10^{26}$ on uniform inputs. The method extends to metrics of bounded doubling dimension and to compact domains with effective geometric routines, including filled simple polygons. At $s=2$, exact decision on metrics with nonzero distances in $\{1,2\}$ is W[1]-complete in $k$. A gap that shrinks with $k$ rules out a deterministic EPAS on unrestricted metrics unless FPT = W[1].

papers.title: The Monophonic Directed Convexities
papers.abstract: Graph Convexity is a topic with many papers in the literature, especially on the $P_3$, geodesic, and monophonic convexities in undirected graphs. Regarding directed graphs, Erd{\H o}s et al. in 1972 and Chartrand and Zhang in 2000 obtained the first results on the $P_3$ and geodesic convexities for directed graphs, respectively. In this paper, we start the investigation of monophonic convexity on directed graphs. We define two convexities, the monophonic and the strong monophonic directed convexities, related to the minimal and the induced directed paths, respectively. We show that deciding whether a set is convex is polynomial-time solvable in the monophonic convexity, but coNP-complete in the strong monophonic convexity. For both convexities, we prove that the hull number is NP-complete even in DAGs. Regarding the monophonic convexity, we prove that the hull number is polynomial time solvable in tournaments, but the interval number is NP-complete in tournaments and also in bipartite oriented graphs.

papers.title: You Can Have It All: Small sparse induced-universal graphs for minor-closed classes
papers.abstract: We show that, for every fixed proper minor-closed graph class $\mathcal{G}$ and every positive integer $n$, there exists a graph $U_n$ with $n^{1+o(1)}$ vertices and edges such that every $n$-vertex graph in $\mathcal{G}$ is isomorphic to an induced subgraph of $U_n$. This result generalizes and unifies the results of Dujmović et al. (J. ACM 2021) on induced-universal graphs and the results of Esperet, Joret, and Morin (J. London Math. Soc. 2023) on sparse induced-universal graphs from planar graphs to all proper minor-closed graph classes. It simultaneously improves the previous bounds for the number of vertices in induced-universal graphs (previously $O(n^2)$ obtained as a corollary of a result of DeVos et al. (J. Comb. Theory, Ser. {B} 2004) and a result of Gavoille and Labourel (ESA 2007)) and the number of edges in subgraph-universal graphs (previously $O(n^{3/2})$ by Babai et al. (Theory and Practice of Combinatorics 1982)).

papers.title: List Update with Per-Page Maximum Delay
papers.abstract: We study list update with per-page maximum delay. Requests may wait, and one access clears all pending requests of a page at its current list rank, paying their maximum waiting penalty. Each service can change the permutation and therefore the cost of later accesses. We give a strictly $5$-competitive deterministic algorithm: serve a page when the oldest waiting time reaches two thirds of its current rank, then move it to the front. Our main tool is an asynchronous marked-rank coupling that compares different list orders and different service histories. A temporal transfer principle separates this permutation argument from two waiting-cost inequalities. It gives factor $5$ for page-specific superadditive penalties, common calendar rates, and additional hard deadlines; deadlines alone admit factor $3$. Two structural conditions on request-specific penalties give factor $3+2κ$. In particular, nonincreasing request severity retains factor $5$ even with unbounded weight ratios. For linear delay, offline optimization is NP-complete but fixed-parameter tractable in the number of pages. We characterize fixed-list batching, show an $Ω(m)$ gap between the best static order and dynamic reordering, and prove that the optimal deterministic factor for one page is exactly $2$. Counterexamples delineate the threshold rule's scope.

papers.title: Online Network Design with Maximum Delay and Stochastic Arrivals
papers.abstract: We study online network services that combine pending requests into batches. Each batch pays for its spatial service and for the waiting time of its oldest request. The objective is the sum of these costs over all batches. Thus requests can share both a spatial purchase and one maximum-delay charge. We assume independent Poisson arrivals of known rates, while actual requests are revealed only upon arrival. For stateless services, suppose that each type has an attainable minimum cost when served alone, that every batch costs at least the stand-alone minimum of each type it contains, and that one finite-cost action can serve any batch, regardless of its request multiplicities. We give a deterministic algorithm with long-run ratio of expectations $e/(e-1)$ against an unrestricted offline optimum. This factor is optimal, even allowing randomization, already at one request location. The key comparison measures the union of time intervals associated with requests. The theorem applies directly to multi-root and pair aggregation on trees. We also study facility location, where each request pays its own connection distance and the bounded-action assumption can fail. A deterministic policy gives a ratio $3$ for arbitrary nonnegative opening costs. It immediately serves a finite initial set of requests, computes an assignment from their observed arrival gaps, and then keeps that assignment fixed. Its analysis combines Poisson insertion with a time-slice packing bound on the offline optimum. Every guarantee includes the full cost of completing finite inputs without an end-of-input signal.

papers.title: Pair-Merge Tokenisation Is Hard to Approximate on Binary Strings and Strongly NP-Hard on Unary Datasets
papers.abstract: Tokenisers such as Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) shorten text by repeatedly merging an adjacent pair of symbols into a new one; fewer tokens mean less computation. We ask whether an efficient algorithm can choose $k$ merges that leave a string of length $n$ almost as short as possible; doing nothing is already within a factor $n$. We prove that, unless P = NP, no polynomial-time algorithm comes within a factor $c\,n/\log n$, for some constant $c>0$, already for one binary string and for BPE-style merges that replace every occurrence. The key idea is that $k$ merges form a grammar with $k$ rules: a vertex-cover gap becomes a grammar-size gap, which we amplify with relabelled copies, encode in binary and realise with explicit merges. For merges that may skip occurrences, a simple algorithm achieves $O(n/\log\log n)$, and no Karp reduction can prove hardness beyond order $n/\log n$ unless coNP $\subseteq$ NP/poly. Over a one-letter alphabet, both tokenisation problems left open by Kastreva et al. are strongly NP-complete on datasets with repeated strings.

papers.title: Stochastic Aggregation with Prescribed Resources and Additive Delay
papers.abstract: We study online aggregation with prescribed resources and additive delay. In this problem, we are given a finite set of resources with purchase costs and a collection of request types, each specifying the resources it requires. Requests arrive over time, and each request can be served immediately or postponed to a later time. A service may serve several pending requests together by purchasing every resource required by at least one of them, paying for each purchased resource only once. These purchases serve only the current batch; resources needed in a later service must be purchased again. A request served $t$ units of time after its arrival incurs delay cost $t$. The objective is to serve all requests while minimizing the sum of resource purchase costs and individual delay costs. We consider a stochastic version of this problem in which requests of each type follow an independent Poisson process of known rate. An online algorithm knows these rates but observes requests only upon arrival. We compare its expected cost with that of an offline optimum that knows the entire realized input and may choose every batch freely. A resource--scale linear program supplies both an offline lower certificate and synchronized service periods. This yields a deterministic online algorithm with polynomial-time preprocessing on rational input and a long-run ratio of expectations below $2.113$. The guarantee applies in particular to rooted multi-level aggregation and prescribed-pair aggregation on trees. Besides, for Poisson TCP acknowledgment, we further characterize the optimal long-run ratio of expectations at every load, showing that its worst-case value is approximately 1.409 and is attained by a deterministic online policy.

papers.title: Local Modifications of Nearest-Neighbor and Min-Plus Representations
papers.abstract: We study how changing a Boolean-valued function at $d$ inputs affects the size and precision of its exact representations. Starting from a representation of size $m$, we prove four bounds, two for nearest-neighbor (NN) representations and two for integer min-plus representations. (i) For NN representations on a finite subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ with $n\ge2$, at most $m+2d$ anchors suffice. The coefficient $2$ is optimal: on a three-point domain, changing one value can increase the minimum number of anchors from one to three. (ii) For NN representations on the Boolean cube with rational anchors, let $R$ be the maximum original coordinate bit length, and let $Δ$ be the maximum bit length of the least common denominator of any one original anchor's coordinates. We construct a representation with at most $m+3d$ anchors on a common dyadic grid and coordinate bit length $O(R+Δ+\log(n+1))$. (iii) For integer min-plus representations on the Boolean cube, we give a construction that keeps the original $m$ forms and their labels and adds at most $d$ new forms. Its maximum weight is at most $W+2n$, where $W$ is the largest absolute original coefficient, including constant terms. (iv) For integer min-plus representations on a finite rational domain $X\subset\mathbb{Q}^n$, at most $m+2d$ forms suffice. Their maximum weight is polynomially bounded in $m,d,W,n,|X|$, the coordinate bound, and the common denominator of $X$. The coefficient $2$ is again optimal: on a three-point domain, changing one value can increase the minimum number of forms from one to three. These bounds imply stability under polynomially many changes on the cube for polynomial-size representations, including those with polynomially bounded NN coordinate bit length or min-plus weight.

papers.title: Online Network Design with Additive Delays and Poisson Arrivals
papers.abstract: We study online service systems in which requests arrive at locations in a network. A service may open a facility and connect customers, buy a subtree linking them to a root, or send a mobile server to visit them. Combining requests can save opening, network, or travel costs, but each request pays its own waiting time. The objective is the sum of these spatial costs and individual delays. We assume independent Poisson arrivals of known rates. The algorithms know how often requests occur, but observe them only upon arrival. We show that these rates suffice to make fixed spatial choices that compete with an offline optimum free to adapt to the realized input. We obtain long-run ratios of expectations below $27.249$ for facility location in finite metrics, $94.415$ for multi-root aggregation on trees, and $24.326$ for online service on trees. All three algorithms are deterministic; the multi-root algorithm also has polynomial-time preprocessing on rational inputs. The proofs connect rate-based spatial choices with lower bounds on unavoidable purchase, movement, and waiting costs. All main proofs are self-contained, and every guarantee includes the full cost of completing finite inputs.

papers.title: Uniform Quantum Average-Case Fine-Grained Hardness of Arithmetized $k$-Orthogonal Vectors
papers.abstract: We study exact evaluation of the arithmetized $k$-Orthogonal Vectors polynomial $FOV^k$ of Ball et al. (2017, 2018). For every fixed integer $k \geq 3$, set $d(n) = \left \lceil \log^2 n \right \rceil$. Assuming the basic decision version of Quantum Strong Exponential-Time Hypothesis (QSETH), for every constant $\varepsilon > 0$, no uniform quantum algorithm runs in $O(n^{k/2 - \varepsilon})$ time on every input and evaluates this polynomial correctly with probability at least $3 / 4$ over a uniformly random input in $\mathbb F_{p(n)}^{knd(n)}$ and the algorithm's internal randomness, for all sufficiently large $n$. This holds when $p(n)$ is the smallest prime greater than $n^{k - 1}$ and when it is the smallest prime greater than $n^k$. Our direct reduction combines classical polynomial self-correction with calls to a quantum average-case evaluator. For the smaller prime, random sampling finds an orthogonal tuple with constant probability whenever the count is large enough to wrap around modulo $p(n)$; otherwise, the exact residue determines the answer. For the larger prime, quantum minimum finding and an asymptotic prime-gap bound account for the cost of generating the prescribed field. In view of prior isolation-based reductions permitting small characteristics, we present these results as explicit reductions for the two canonical-prime families, with all setup costs included in the uniform quantum running time. The hardness guarantee concerns single-instance exact evaluation; a matching quantum evaluation algorithm and a quantum proof-of-work protocol remain open.

papers.title: Bounded Weighted Edit Distance with Metric Costs
papers.abstract: We give a deterministic $O(n+k^2)$-time algorithm for bounded weighted edit distance when the input costs form an integer metric on the alphabet extended by a gap symbol. Here $n$ is the total input length and $k$ is the given threshold on the distance. If the distance is at most $k$, the algorithm returns it with an optimal alignment. Otherwise, it reports that the distance exceeds $k$. The running time matches the classical unit-cost bound and is independent of the alphabet size and of the largest cost. The algorithm keeps only the farthest-reaching prefix alignment for each cost and each difference between the total gap costs of the aligned prefixes. For real metrics whose nonzero costs are at least one, scaling and upward rounding give a $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation for the bounded problem in $\widetilde{O}(n+(k/\varepsilon)^2)$ time. If insertions and deletions have integer costs, the running time improves to $\widetilde{O}(n+k^2/\varepsilon)$.

papers.title: Solomonoff Induction with Reflective Oracles
papers.abstract: We study predictive properties of a reflective variant of Solomonoff induction formulated using reflective oracles (Fallenstein et al. 2015, Wyeth et al. 2025). We show that the resulting optimal predictor succeeds against computable predictive strategies that specify only part of the data-generating process. The argument relies on the fact that hypotheses computable from the predictor's own conditional probabilities remain within the reflective hypothesis class. In particular, the predictor learns incomplete models specified by computable interval restrictions on next-bit probabilities. We also establish weighted forms of unbiasedness and calibration. Finally, we discuss whether an optimal predictor's conditional probabilities suffice to compute every hypothesis in the reflective class.

papers.title: Directed Singular-Value Sparsifiers with $O(n \log n/ε^2)$ Arcs
papers.abstract: Given an unweighted directed graph, a sparsifier is a nonnegative reweighting of original arcs that preserves every in-degree and out-degree exactly. In this work, we study singular-value sparsifiers, which are generalizations of spectral sparsifiers. Singular-value sparsifiers find a number of applications in theoretical computer science, such as maintaining directed cuts and flows, speeding up directed Laplacian solvers, and sparsifying dense weight matrices in neural networks. Strong singular-value (SV) approximation supports sparse representations of directed random walks with guarantees that remain stable under products, and controls bilinear error in the left and right Schur-complement metrics. We prove that every unweighted directed graph on $n$ vertices admits an $\varepsilon$-SV sparsifier with $O(n\log(2n)/\varepsilon^2)$ arcs, improving the $O(n\log^5 n/\varepsilon^2)$ support bound of Lau, Wang, and Zhou. The sparsifier is a nonnegative reweighting of original arcs and preserves every in-degree and out-degree exactly. We also give a randomized construction with $\tilde{O}(m+n)$ real-arithmetic running time, where $m$ is the input support size, and the output has the same support bound and rational weights of polynomial bit length.

papers.title: Optimal radio labelings for the Cartesian product of a path and the Heawood graph
papers.abstract: For a simple graph $G$, let $d(u,v)$ denote the distance between two vertices $u$ and $v$ in $G$, and let $diam(G)$ denote the diameter of $G$. A radio labeling of $G$ is a mapping $f : V(G) \rightarrow \mathbb{N} \cup \{0\}$ such that $|f(u)-f(v)|\geq diam(G) + 1 - d(u,v)$ holds for every pair of distinct vertices $u, v \in G$. The span of $f$ is the difference between the largest and smallest integers assigned by $f$, and the radio number $rn(G)$ is the minimum span taking over all radio labelings of $G$. Let $P_n$ denote the path on $n$ vertices and let $H$ denote the Heawood graph (see Figure-1). In this paper we determine the radio number for the Cartesian product of a path and the Heawood graph, and characterize all optimal radio labelings of $P_n \Box H$. Moreover, we show that the radio number of $P_n \Box H$ exceed the lower bound given for $rn(G)$ in [6], where $G$ is any graph, and that this gap is arbitrarily large.

papers.title: $\mathsf{SVP}_\infty$ Is NP-Hard for Power-of-two Cyclotomic Ideals
papers.abstract: We prove that exact decision-$\mathsf{SVP}$ in the coefficient $\ell_\infty$-norm is $\mathsf{NP}$-complete for principal ideals and free modules of rank two over the cyclotomic rings $R_n=\mathbb{Z}[X]/(X^n+1)$, where $n$ ranges over powers of two. For each case, we give a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction from the Subset Sum problem. For an instance with $s$ positive input integers, the output lattice has dimension $O(s)$. A solution to the original Subset Sum instance can be recovered in polynomial time from any nonzero output lattice vector of norm at most the specified bound. We also transfer these reductions from $R_n$ to the power-of-two cyclic rings $S_{2n}=\mathbb{Z}[X]/(X^{2n}-1)$. This gives $\mathsf{NP}$-completeness of decision-$\mathsf{SVP}$ in the coefficient $\ell_\infty$-norm for principal ideals and free modules of any fixed positive rank over these rings.

papers.title: Adversarial risk analysis with fully probabilistic designs
papers.abstract: Adversarial risk analysis (ARA) informs decision-makers when facing intelligent opponents and uncertain outcomes, enabling an analyst to model beliefs about the opponents' preferences, capabilities, beliefs, and the strategic calculations that opponents employ. Major applications cover reliability and risk analysis of critical infrastructures in presence of adversarial threats. In such domains, ARA mitigates typical common knowledge assumptions of standard game-theoretic approaches. However, ARA entails complex modelling and computations. To alleviate these, we explore its combination with fully probabilistic design (FPD), a control theory methodology supporting an agent in choosing the decision distribution that achieves the outcomes with a distribution closest to its ideal. We use FPD to model and forecast the opponent's decisions within an ARA setting and present how to handle security games within this ARA-FPD framework, covering both single and multiple stage problems.

papers.title: Mixed-integer dual network problems are solvable in strongly polynomial time
papers.abstract: In this paper we show that mixed-integer linear programming is solvable in strongly polynomial time if the constraint matrix is totally unimodular with at most two nonzero entries in every row. This is done by reducing the problem to an instance of minimization of an $L$-convex function.

papers.title: Quantum-Assisted Counterfactual Regret Minimization for Bounded-Payoff Imperfect-Information Games
papers.abstract: Imperfect-information games with a graded-reward structure present significant computational challenges for equilibrium computation, since the payoff expectations must be estimated across exponentially large strategy spaces. Counterfactual Regret Minimization over the years has proven effective for approximating Nash equilibria, but Monte Carlo variants create a large overhead of sampling costs when the counterfactual values are estimated from sampled game-tree trajectories. We propose a novel Quantum-Assisted Counterfactual Regret Minimization, a framework that uses Quantum Amplitude Estimation to reduce the computational complexity of the regret updates in bounded-payoff imperfect-information games, while preserving the convergence of its classical counterpart. We give a theoretical analysis of the resulting exploitability bound, discuss NISQ-compatible amplitude-estimation variants, the structure of their resource requirements, and outline what is needed to validate the potential advantage empirically.

papers.title: Complexity of Deciding Existence of Maltsev Polymorphisms of Finite Relational Structures
papers.abstract: In this article, we show that the problem of deciding whether a finite relational structure $\mathbf{A}$ admits a Maltsev polymorphism is a computational problem, which can be solved in polynomial time. We provide a proof of this result by reducing the problem to deciding whether a binary relational structure, associated with $\mathbf{A}$ admits such a polymorphism. In our construction of such an algorithm, we make an extensive use of a property of binary relations, which is implied by the existence of a Maltsev polymorphism, the so-called rectangularity property.

papers.title: From Worst-Case to Smoothed Complexity in Continuous Optimization
papers.abstract: Worst-case complexity bounds often fail to reflect the practical performance of optimization algorithms, while average-case complexity heavily relies on the distribution of the input. In this work, we develop a smoothed-analysis framework for classical continuous optimization algorithms by studying their behaviour on random perturbations of arbitrary functions. Our main contribution is to apply methods suited for non-degenerate functions to perturbations of degenerate functions, thereby recovering the faster best-known rates for the non-degenerate class. We derive smoothed complexity guarantees for several standard methods, including (Accelerated) Gradient Descent, Conjugate Gradient, and Newton-type methods, under various settings including nonconvex ones, and show that these bounds can substantially improve upon their worst-case guarantees, bringing them closer to the practical behaviour of the respective methods.

papers.title: A note on the intractability of enumerating the maximal satisfiable subformulas of a Horn expression
papers.abstract: We show that, given a Horn expression and a family of inclusion-wise maximal satisfiable subsets of its clauses, deciding whether there exists another maximal satisfiable subset is NP-complete. As a consequence, unless P=NP, there is no output-polynomial time algorithm enumerating the maximal satisfiable subformulas of a Horn expression.

papers.title: Linear-size graphs at every strict dismantling level
papers.abstract: Dismantling reduces a graph to one vertex by successive deletions. At level zero, a vertex is eligible if one of its neighbours is adjacent to all its other neighbours. At level $k\geq1$, its neighbours must induce a graph dismantlable at level $k-1$. A graph has strict level $k$ if it admits a reduction at level $k$ and none at level $k-1$. For every $k\geq1$, we construct a graph of strict level $k$ with $3k+8$ vertices. Each step adds three vertices: the neighbours of one induce the preceding graph, and the other two provide the adjacencies used to rule out other first deletions at the lower level. A second construction gives a graph of order $4k+4$ at strict level $k$. Together the two families give the upper bound $\min\{4k+4,3k+8\}$ on the least order at strict level $k$.
